options.rationale: Urine sitting still allows infection and stone formation, which is how stasis presents.

options.text: A specific gravity of 1.015
options.rationale: Within the normal range and not a sign of stasis.

questions.takeaway: Urinary stasis raises infection risk and allows stones to form.

questions.stem: A patient in traction cannot move the affected leg but is able to exercise the other limbs. Which exercise maintains strength in the immobilized leg?

options.text: Isotonic exercise, contracting the muscle while the joint moves
options.rationale: Requires joint movement, which traction prevents.

options.text: Passive range of motion performed by the nurse
options.rationale: Maintains flexibility. The patient's muscle does no work, so no strength is built.

options.text: Resistance training with ankle weights
options.rationale: Adds load through a moving joint, which is not possible or safe here.

options.text: Isometric exercise, contracting the muscle without moving the joint
options.rationale: Builds static strength and joint stability and is safe around painful or healing tissue.

questions.takeaway: Isotonic moves the joint. Isometric does not, which is why it works in a limb that must stay still.

questions.stem: Which factors influence a patient's level of activity? Select all that apply.

options.text: Environment
options.rationale: Stairs, terrain, and access decide what movement is possible.

options.text: Social support
options.rationale: Determines whether someone has help and encouragement to stay active.

options.text: Developmental stage
options.rationale: Named among the influences on activity. What is expected differs across the lifespan.

options.text: Blood type
options.rationale: Has no relationship to activity or mobility.

options.text: Culture
options.rationale: Shapes which activities are valued and considered appropriate.

questions.takeaway: Activity is shaped by development, health status, lifestyle, culture, environment, behavior, and social support.

questions.stem: A patient recovering from pneumonia has been in bed for four days. Which action best prevents respiratory complications of immobility?

options.text: Assist the patient to sit upright and cough and deep breathe
options.rationale: Sitting upright increases lung expansion and coughing clears retained secretions, which are the two failures behind atelectasis.

options.text: Apply sequential compression devices to both legs
options.rationale: Prevents venous stasis and thrombus. It does nothing for the lungs.

options.text: Perform passive range of motion to all extremities
options.rationale: Prevents contractures. Correct care, different system.

options.text: Increase dietary protein intake
options.rationale: Addresses negative nitrogen balance, not lung expansion.

questions.takeaway: Match the intervention to the mechanism. Secretions pooling needs expansion and coughing.

questions.stem: A patient on bed rest for four days is preparing to ambulate. Supine blood pressure is 128/76 with a pulse of 78. After sitting at the edge of the bed for one minute, blood pressure is 102/58 with a pulse of 104 and the patient reports the room is spinning. Which action does the nurse take?

options.text: Assist the patient to stand so the episode resolves with movement
options.rationale: Standing raises the head further above the heart and deepens the drop in cerebral perfusion. This is the moment a fall happens.

options.text: Keep the patient sitting and supported, then recheck before standing
options.rationale: A drop in pressure with a compensating rise in rate on sitting is orthostatic hypotension. Staying seated lets the circulation catch up without abandoning the activity, and the recheck is the checkpoint before the riskiest part.

options.text: Return the patient to supine and cancel activity for the day
options.rationale: Abandoning the activity treats the symptom by deepening the deconditioning that caused it.

options.text: Administer the ordered analgesic and reattempt in one hour
options.rationale: Nothing in the findings describes pain, and an hour of additional rest does not improve orthostatic tolerance.

questions.takeaway: Read the pair together: falling pressure with a rising rate on position change is orthostatic hypotension. Stage the change, do not cancel it.

questions.stem: A patient has been immobile for five days after a pelvic fracture. The nurse notes that the left calf is 3 cm larger than the right and is warm and tender. Which action does the nurse take first?

options.text: Apply the sequential compression devices to both legs
options.rationale: Compression prevents venous stasis in a limb without a clot. Applying it now treats prevention as if it were treatment.

options.text: Encourage active ankle pumping in both legs every hour
options.rationale: Leg exercises are correct prevention and are not the response to a limb that already shows the complication.

options.text: Hold the sequential compression devices and notify the provider
options.rationale: Unilateral calf swelling with warmth and tenderness suggests a thrombus has already formed. Compression on a limb with a suspected clot is applied only after evaluation, so the device is held and the finding is reported.

options.text: Measure both calves again in four hours to establish a trend
options.rationale: The difference is already measured and symptomatic. Waiting adds risk without adding information.

questions.takeaway: Prevention and treatment are different. Once one limb shows swelling, warmth, and tenderness, stop preventing and start reporting.

questions.stem: A patient who slides down in bed several times a day has an area of reddened, partially denuded skin over the sacrum. The bed is routinely kept at 45 degrees. Which change most directly addresses the mechanism causing this injury?

options.text: Apply a moisture barrier ointment to the sacrum twice daily
options.rationale: Moisture management is appropriate skin care and does nothing about the sliding that is tearing tissue.

options.text: Turn the patient every two hours without changing the bed angle
options.rationale: Turning limits time under pressure. The injury here is produced by sliding, which continues at 45 degrees.

options.text: Place a pillow under the knees to improve comfort
options.rationale: Knee flexion does help resist sliding, and alone it does not address either the bed angle or how the patient is moved.

options.text: Lower the head of the bed when clinically possible and use a lift sheet to reposition
options.rationale: Elevation lets the skeleton slide while the skin stays fixed, which is shear, and dragging adds friction. Lowering the angle removes the driving force and lifting removes the surface drag.

questions.takeaway: Pressure pushes down, friction rubs, shear slides the tissue under fixed skin. A head-up bed plus dragging produces the last two.

questions.stem: A patient immobile for two weeks has a footboard in place. The nurse finds the feet resting with the toes pointed and a gap of several inches between the soles and the board. Which conclusion does the nurse draw?

options.text: The device is not in contact with the feet, so it is not preventing plantar flexion
options.rationale: A footboard works only when the soles rest against it at a neutral angle. A gap means the ankles are free to settle into plantar flexion, which is how foot drop develops.

options.text: The findings are expected and the device is working as intended
options.rationale: Toes pointed is the position the device exists to prevent, so the finding is evidence it is not working.

options.text: The patient has developed a permanent contracture that the device can now correct
options.rationale: Contractures are permanent shortening. Positioning prevents them and does not reverse them, and nothing here establishes one has formed yet.

options.text: The gap indicates the patient has been performing active ankle exercises
options.rationale: Active movement would show the ankles in varied positions, not both settled in plantar flexion.

questions.takeaway: A supportive device only works in contact. Check that the intervention is actually happening, not just present.

questions.stem: A patient immobile for three weeks eats about a third of each meal. Serum albumin has fallen from 3.8 to 2.9 g/dL, weight is down 4 kg, and the arms and legs appear visibly thinner. Which process best explains this pattern?

options.text: Fluid volume deficit producing the weight loss
options.rationale: Dehydration would raise albumin through hemoconcentration rather than lower it, and it does not thin the extremities.

options.text: Negative nitrogen balance from immobility compounded by reduced intake
options.rationale: Immobility drives protein breakdown beyond intake, and decreased appetite is itself a listed metabolic effect. Falling albumin with visible loss of lean mass is that process made measurable.

options.text: Increased metabolic demand from prolonged bed rest
options.rationale: Immobility lowers metabolic demand. The direction is reversed.

options.text: Altered calcium metabolism causing muscle wasting
options.rationale: Altered calcium metabolism produces bone demineralization and a rising serum calcium, not loss of muscle protein.

questions.takeaway: Immobility takes protein apart while appetite falls. Albumin down, weight down, limbs thinner is one process, not three.

questions.stem: A patient two days after knee arthroplasty is on a weight-bearing restriction and reports the knee is too painful to bend beyond a few degrees. Which exercise best maintains quadriceps strength now?

options.text: Perform straight leg raises through the full range
options.rationale: Isotonic work through a full arc. The hip moves and the load on a painful healing knee exceeds what this patient tolerates.

options.text: Have the nurse move the knee through its full range twice daily
options.rationale: Passive range maintains flexibility and the patient's muscle does no work, so no strength is built.

options.text: Tighten the quadriceps and hold without moving the knee
options.rationale: Isometric contraction loads the muscle with no joint movement, which is why it is used around painful or healing joints. Strength and joint stability are preserved during the period the knee cannot move.

options.text: Walk short distances with a walker several times daily
options.rationale: Isotonic and appropriate later. It conflicts with the weight-bearing restriction stated in the stem.

questions.takeaway: Isotonic moves the joint, isometric does not. When the joint cannot move, isometric is the only way to keep the muscle.

questions.stem: A nurse repositions an immobile patient from supine to a 30-degree side-lying position with pillows supporting the back, between the knees, and under the upper arm. Which outcomes does this positioning achieve? Select all that apply.

options.text: Maintains body alignment
options.rationale: Support at the back, knees, and arm holds the trunk and limbs in alignment instead of letting them collapse into the mattress.

options.text: Reduces pressure over the sacrum
options.rationale: Turning shifts weight off the tissue that was bearing it, which limits time under load.

options.text: Prevents hip and knee contracture by holding the joints out of fixed flexion
options.rationale: A pillow between the knees keeps the upper leg from adducting and the hips from settling into a fixed position.

options.text: Supports lung expansion compared with a flat supine position
options.rationale: Position determines how far the lungs can expand, and a supported side-lying position relieves pressure on the dependent lung compared with lying flat.

options.text: Eliminates the need for scheduled range-of-motion exercises
options.rationale: Position and movement do different jobs. Holding a joint correctly does not carry it through its arc.

options.text: Restores muscle strength lost during the period of bed rest
options.rationale: Strength returns with loading and activity. No position rebuilds muscle.

questions.takeaway: Positioning maintains alignment, supports breathing, protects skin, promotes comfort, prevents contractures, supports function. It does not replace movement.

questions.stem: A patient with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease has an arterial blood gas showing pH 7.36, PaCO2 58 mm Hg, and HCO3 32 mEq/L. How does the nurse interpret this result?

options.text: Normal blood gas, no action needed
options.rationale: The pH is normal and nothing else is. Two abnormal values with a normal pH is the signature of compensation, not health.

options.text: Fully compensated respiratory acidosis
options.rationale: The CO2 is high, which acidifies. The bicarbonate is high, which is the kidney buffering it. The pH has been pulled back inside the range, so compensation is complete.

options.text: Partially compensated metabolic alkalosis
options.rationale: A metabolic alkalosis would start with a raised bicarbonate and a raised pH. The pH is not alkalotic and the CO2 elevation is the primary problem, not the compensation.

options.text: Uncompensated respiratory acidosis
options.rationale: Uncompensated means the pH is still abnormal and the metabolic value is still normal. Here the bicarbonate has already moved and the pH has come back.

questions.takeaway: A pH inside the normal range with an abnormal CO2 and an abnormal bicarbonate is full compensation, and it means a chronic problem underneath.
questions.strategy: The normal pH is bait. Read the other two numbers before you decide the patient is fine.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: It is 7.36, normal but sitting on the acidic side of 7.40.
58 is high, so the lung is the problem and the direction is acidosis.
32 is high, moving opposite the pH, which makes it compensation.

elimination.verdict: Respiratory acidosis, fully compensated. A normal pH does not mean a normal patient.

questions.stem: A patient has been vomiting for three days. Which acid-base disturbance does the nurse anticipate?

options.text: Metabolic acidosis
options.rationale: Metabolic acidosis comes from losing bicarbonate below the stomach, which is diarrhea, or from gaining acid, which is ketoacidosis or renal failure.

options.text: Metabolic alkalosis
options.rationale: Gastric contents are hydrochloric acid. Vomiting removes acid from the body, so what is left is relatively alkaline.

options.text: Respiratory acidosis
options.rationale: Respiratory problems change the CO2. Vomiting does not affect ventilation directly.

options.text: Respiratory alkalosis
options.rationale: Respiratory alkalosis comes from blowing off CO2, which is hyperventilation, not vomiting.

questions.takeaway: Vomiting loses acid and causes alkalosis. Diarrhea loses bicarbonate and causes acidosis. They are opposites and they are tested as a pair.
questions.strategy: Two options are metabolic and two are respiratory. The stem gives you a gastrointestinal loss, so the metabolic pair is where the answer lives.

strategies: Opposite pair, look closely
Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Metabolic versus respiratory. Vomiting is not a breathing problem.
Stomach contents are acid.
Lose acid, become alkalotic.

elimination.verdict: Metabolic alkalosis. The mirror item gives you diarrhea and the answer flips to acidosis.

questions.stem: Which assessment gives the nurse the most reliable early evidence that a patient with heart failure is retaining fluid?

options.text: Daily weight taken at the same time on the same scale
options.rationale: A liter of fluid weighs about one kilogram, or 2.2 pounds. The scale registers the gain before edema is visible and before crackles appear.

options.text: Presence of pitting edema in the ankles
options.rationale: Edema is real but late. Several liters can accumulate before the tissue shows it, and dependent edema also varies with position and time of day.

options.text: Crackles heard in the lung bases
options.rationale: Crackles mean fluid has already reached the lungs. That is a finding you act on, not an early warning.

options.text: Patient report of thirst and dry mouth
options.rationale: Thirst points toward deficit rather than excess, and thirst is unreliable in older adults because the thirst mechanism blunts with age.

questions.takeaway: Weight is the honest number. One kilogram equals one liter, and the scale changes before edema or crackles do. Same time, same scale, same clothing.
questions.strategy: Three options are findings that appear after the fluid has already collected. Only one of them catches it on the way in.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Ask which finding appears first.
Both are late and both require a volume that has already accumulated.
It points the wrong direction and it is unreliable in older adults.

elimination.verdict: Daily weight. It is the earliest and the most reproducible.

questions.stem: An 82-year-old is admitted from home after two days of poor oral intake in a heat wave. Which findings support a diagnosis of fluid volume deficit? Select all that apply.

options.text: Heart rate 112 and blood pressure 96/58
options.rationale: The earliest compensation for a falling volume is tachycardia, and the blood pressure drops once compensation is exhausted.

options.text: Urine output 15 mL/hr, dark and concentrated
options.rationale: Below 30 mL/hr is oliguria. The kidney is conserving everything it can, and concentrating the urine is how it does that.

options.text: New confusion since yesterday
options.rationale: New confusion in an older adult is a laboratory and perfusion question before it is a cognitive one. It is frequently the first thing a family notices.

options.text: Tenting of the skin on the back of the hand
options.rationale: Aging skin tents on the hand and forearm whether or not the patient is dry. Assess turgor over the sternum or the forehead instead.

options.text: Jugular venous distention while sitting upright
options.rationale: That is a sign of excess, not deficit. Flat neck veins would fit this patient.

options.text: Weight loss of 3 kg since last week
options.rationale: Three kilograms is about three liters. Acute weight change is fluid, not tissue.

questions.takeaway: Deficit shows up as tachycardia first, then hypotension, with concentrated low-volume urine, acute weight loss and new confusion. Hand turgor and thirst are both unreliable in older adults.
questions.strategy: Two options are written to look like assessment skill. One tests turgor at the wrong site and one describes the opposite problem.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.action: Take the vital signs and the urine
steps.detail: Both fit a falling circulating volume.
Acute change of this size is water.
Wrong site for an 82-year-old.
That belongs to overload.

elimination.verdict: A, B, C and F. The two rejected options are the ones that feel most like assessment.

questions.scenario: A nurse reviews the intravenous fluids prescribed for four patients on a medical unit.
questions.stem: For each fluid, indicate its tonicity relative to plasma.

rows.text: 0.9% sodium chloride, prescribed after several hours of vomiting
rows.rationale: Same osmolality as plasma, so it produces no net shift and stays in the space you infuse it into. That is what a patient who lost extracellular fluid needs.

rows.text: 0.45% sodium chloride, prescribed for cellular dehydration
rows.rationale: Lower osmolality than plasma, so water moves into the cells. Useful for rehydrating cells and dangerous in anyone at risk of cerebral edema.

rows.text: 3% sodium chloride, prescribed for symptomatic hyponatremia with seizures
rows.rationale: Higher osmolality than plasma, so it pulls water out of the cells. Given slowly and with close monitoring, because correcting sodium quickly causes osmotic demyelination.

rows.text: Lactated Ringer solution, prescribed for a patient with burns
rows.rationale: An isotonic balanced crystalloid. It expands the circulating volume without shifting fluid across the cell membrane.

questions.takeaway: Isotonic stays put and expands the vascular space. Hypotonic moves water into cells. Hypertonic pulls water out of them.
questions.strategy: Sort by the percentage against 0.9%, which is the isotonic reference. Below it moves water in, above it pulls water out.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: That is isotonic, and so is lactated Ringer.
Less than 0.9% is hypotonic, more than 0.9% is hypertonic.
Cellular dehydration needs water in; cerebral edema needs water out.

elimination.verdict: Two isotonic, one hypotonic, one hypertonic.

questions.stem: A nurse receives an order reading: potassium chloride 20 mEq IV push now for a serum potassium of 2.9 mEq/L. What is the nurse's best action?

options.text: Administer it slowly over five minutes with the patient on a monitor
options.rationale: The trap. Administering a lethal route more carefully does not make it safe. There is no safe rate for IV push potassium.

options.text: Dilute it and infuse it over one hour through a peripheral line
options.rationale: Wrong twice. Diluting is the right idea and 20 mEq over one hour is 20 mEq/hr, double the peripheral maximum of 10 mEq/hr. Rewriting an unsafe order is also prescribing, which is not the nurse's to do.

options.text: Hold the dose and contact the prescriber to clarify the order
options.rationale: Potassium is never given IV push. The nurse who recognizes an unsafe order stops and questions it, and carrying out an unsafe order does not transfer the responsibility.

options.text: Give it orally instead, since the patient can swallow
options.rationale: Changing the route is prescribing. The recognition is correct and the action exceeds the nurse's scope.

questions.takeaway: IV push potassium is fatal. The correct response to an unsafe order is to question it, never to carry it out more carefully or to substitute your own version.
questions.strategy: Three options all find a way to give the drug. Only one of them stops.

strategies: Priority key word
Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Potassium is never pushed.
A slower push and a nurse-chosen dilution are both still acting on an unsafe order.
That is prescribing.

elimination.verdict: Hold and clarify. Reject the rate, not the technique.

questions.stem: Fifteen minutes into a unit of packed red blood cells, a patient develops chills, a temperature rise from 37.0 C to 38.6 C, and low back pain. What does the nurse do first?

options.text: Slow the infusion and continue to monitor
options.rationale: Slowing keeps incompatible blood going in. Every minute of continued infusion adds to the hemolysis.

options.text: Stop the transfusion and keep the line open with normal saline using new tubing
options.rationale: Stop first. Then maintain access with saline through fresh tubing, because running saline through the existing set would push the blood remaining in the line into the patient.

options.text: Administer the prescribed acetaminophen for the fever
options.rationale: Treats a symptom of a reaction that is still running. The drug never comes before stopping the cause.

options.text: Obtain a urine specimen to check for hemoglobinuria
options.rationale: It will be needed, and it is not first. Collecting a specimen while the transfusion continues is assessment at the expense of the patient.

questions.takeaway: When something goes wrong during an infusion or a transfusion, the first action is always to stop it. Assess, notify and document all come after.
questions.strategy: All four options are things that happen during this event. The question is only about order.

strategies: Priority key word
Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Stop before you call.
Reducing an exposure is not removing it.

steps.action: Cut the drug and the specimen
steps.detail: Both are correct later and neither is first.

elimination.verdict: Stop the transfusion, then saline through new tubing to the hub.

questions.stem: A patient in the emergency department is breathing 36 times a minute after a panic attack and reports tingling around the mouth and in both hands. Which explanation does the nurse give?

options.text: The calcium level has dropped and needs replacement
options.rationale: The total calcium has not changed. Alkalosis increases calcium binding to albumin, which lowers the ionized fraction without lowering the number on the lab report.

options.text: Rapid breathing has lowered the carbon dioxide and raised the blood pH
options.rationale: Hyperventilation blows off CO2, which produces respiratory alkalosis. Alkalosis shifts calcium onto albumin, and less free calcium means irritable nerves.

options.text: Oxygen levels have fallen and the tissues are hypoxic
options.rationale: Hyperventilation raises oxygen, it does not lower it. Nothing here suggests hypoxia.

options.text: Potassium has shifted out of the cells in response to stress
options.rationale: Alkalosis drives potassium into cells, not out. The direction is wrong and potassium does not cause perioral tingling.

questions.takeaway: Perioral and fingertip tingling appears in hypocalcemia, hypomagnesemia and respiratory alkalosis. A hyperventilating patient with tingling lips has a breathing problem.
questions.strategy: Tingling is a strong cue for calcium, which is exactly why the question offers it. Read the respiratory rate before you reach for the electrolyte.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: 36 a minute is the finding the stem is built on.
Fast breathing raises oxygen.
Alkalosis moves potassium in, not out.
The number has not changed, the binding has.

elimination.verdict: Respiratory alkalosis. The calcium option is the trap and it is the one most students pick.

questions.stem: Which conditions would the nurse expect to produce metabolic acidosis? Select all that apply.

options.text: Diabetic ketoacidosis
options.rationale: Ketoacids are added to the blood faster than they can be buffered or excreted.

options.text: Prolonged severe diarrhea
options.rationale: Intestinal contents below the stomach are alkaline. Losing them loses bicarbonate.

options.text: Acute kidney injury with a rising creatinine
options.rationale: The kidney is the organ that excretes fixed acid and regenerates bicarbonate. When it fails, acid accumulates.

options.text: Continuous nasogastric suction
options.rationale: Suction removes gastric acid, the same as vomiting. That produces alkalosis.

options.text: Prolonged hyperventilation from anxiety
options.rationale: That is a respiratory cause, and it produces alkalosis by removing CO2.

options.text: Shock with poor tissue perfusion
options.rationale: Cells without oxygen switch to anaerobic metabolism and produce lactic acid.

questions.takeaway: Metabolic acidosis comes from gaining fixed acid or losing bicarbonate. Ketones, lactate and retained renal acid are gains; diarrhea is the loss.
questions.strategy: Two of the six are alkalosis in disguise, and one of them is respiratory rather than metabolic.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Hyperventilation is a lung mechanism and comes out immediately.

steps.action: Ask gained acid or lost base
steps.detail: Ketoacidosis, kidney injury and shock all gain acid.
Diarrhea loses base. Suction, like vomiting, loses acid.

elimination.verdict: A, B, C and F. Nasogastric suction is the mirror image and produces alkalosis.

questions.stem: Complete each interpretation by selecting from the choices below.
questions.sentence:
A patient with sepsis has pH 7.28, PaCO2 32 mm Hg, HCO3 15 mEq/L. This is [[1]].

A postoperative patient who has been receiving opioids has pH 7.30, PaCO2 54 mm Hg, HCO3 25 mEq/L. This is [[2]].

A patient with three days of nasogastric suction has pH 7.50, PaCO2 42 mm Hg, HCO3 32 mEq/L. This is [[3]].

For the septic patient, the respiratory rate of 30 is best understood as [[4]].

options.text: metabolic acidosis with respiratory compensation
options.rationale: The bicarbonate is low, which is the primary problem, and the pH is acidotic. The low CO2 is the lung blowing off acid to help.

options.text: respiratory acidosis
options.rationale: The CO2 is low, not high. A respiratory acidosis requires retained CO2.

options.text: metabolic alkalosis
options.rationale: The pH is 7.28, which is acidotic.

options.text: a fully compensated disturbance
options.rationale: Full compensation would have returned the pH to normal. It has not.

options.text: respiratory acidosis
options.rationale: The CO2 is high and the pH is low, moving opposite each other, which makes it respiratory. The normal bicarbonate means the kidney has not compensated yet.

options.text: metabolic acidosis
options.rationale: The bicarbonate is normal, so the metabolic side is not the problem.

options.text: respiratory alkalosis
options.rationale: That would show a low CO2 and a high pH.

options.text: a normal blood gas
options.rationale: A pH of 7.30 is below the range.

options.text: metabolic alkalosis
options.rationale: Suction removes gastric acid. The bicarbonate is high and the pH is high, and the CO2 is normal, so the metabolic side is the problem.

options.text: respiratory alkalosis
options.rationale: The CO2 is 42, which is normal. A respiratory alkalosis requires a low CO2.

options.text: metabolic acidosis
options.rationale: The pH is 7.50, which is alkalotic.

options.text: compensated respiratory acidosis
options.rationale: Nothing here is acidotic and the CO2 is normal.

options.text: compensation that should not be slowed
options.rationale: The fast breathing is how the body is offloading acid. Sedating it or slowing it removes the only compensation the patient has.

options.text: a primary respiratory problem needing sedation
options.rationale: The lung is helping, not failing. Slowing it would drive the pH lower.

options.text: anxiety requiring reassurance and rebreathing
options.rationale: That applies to respiratory alkalosis from panic. This patient is acidotic.

options.text: an indication for immediate intubation
options.rationale: Nothing in the values shows a failing airway or failing ventilation.

questions.takeaway: Read the pH, then the CO2, then the bicarbonate. The value moving opposite the pH is the cause; the value moving with it is compensation.
questions.strategy: The last blank is the one that matters clinically. Fast breathing is a cause in respiratory alkalosis and a rescue in metabolic acidosis.

strategies: Match each part to what the stem gives

steps.detail: Acidotic or alkalotic decides half the answer before you read anything else.

steps.action: Find the value moving opposite the pH
steps.detail: That one is the cause.

steps.action: Ask what the other value is doing
steps.detail: Moving with the pH means it is compensating.

elimination.verdict: Metabolic acidosis, respiratory acidosis, metabolic alkalosis, and the fast breathing is compensation you protect rather than treat.

questions.stem: A patient with intact vision and hearing consistently misinterprets what she sees and hears after a stroke. At which stage of sensory experience is her deficit?

options.text: Reception
options.rationale: Reception is the stimulus reaching the receptor. Her eyes and ears are working, so the stimulus is arriving.

options.text: Perception
options.rationale: Perception is the brain organizing and interpreting what arrived. Intact receptors with faulty interpretation places the problem here.

options.text: Reaction
options.rationale: Reaction is what the person does about the stimulus. She is responding, just to a misread signal.

options.text: Adaptation
options.rationale: Adaptation is the normal process of ceasing to notice a constant stimulus, such as no longer feeling your watch.

questions.takeaway: Reception, perception, reaction. A deficit can sit at any of the three, which is why intact eyes do not guarantee accurate sight.
questions.strategy: The stem hands you normal receptors on purpose. That single detail eliminates the first stage.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Vision and hearing both work.
The stimulus is arriving.
Interpretation, which is perception.

elimination.verdict: Perception. The stroke damaged the interpreting, not the sensing.

questions.stem: A patient in intensive care on day three is agitated, cannot follow a sentence, and keeps pulling at the telemetry leads. There is no delirium screening tool result and the neurologic exam is unchanged. Which nursing action does the nurse take first?

options.text: Obtain an order for soft wrist restraints
options.rationale: The trap, and it looks like safety. Restraints treat the behavior and leave the cause running, and every alternative comes first.

options.text: Cluster care and provide an uninterrupted quiet period
options.rationale: The picture is sensory overload: three days of alarms, lights, multiple caregivers and no protected sleep. Reducing input is the intervention that addresses the cause.

options.text: Request a psychiatric consultation for the agitation
options.rationale: Escalates a problem the nurse can address, and it leaves the environment unchanged in the meantime.

options.text: Increase orientation by explaining each piece of equipment in detail
options.rationale: Orientation helps deprivation. This patient is receiving too much input already, so more talking adds to the load.

questions.takeaway: A client pulling at lines because of sensory overload does not need restraints, needs the overload reduced. Least restrictive intervention first, and cluster care is that intervention.
questions.strategy: Two options add something and one removes freedom. Only one option reduces what is actually driving the behavior.

strategies: Priority key word
Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Three days of unrelieved stimulation.
Never before alternatives, and it does not address the cause.
Right for deprivation, wrong for overload.
Escalates before acting.

elimination.verdict: Cluster care and protect sleep. Any item pairing restraints with a less restrictive option is testing least restrictive first.

questions.stem: An 84-year-old nursing home resident is described by staff as "becoming demented." He has been withdrawn, answers questions incorrectly and has stopped joining meals. Which assessments does the nurse perform before accepting that description? Select all that apply.

options.text: Inspect the ear canals for cerumen impaction
options.rationale: Impacted wax is the most common cause of canal obstruction and the most commonly correctable hearing loss in older adults.

options.text: Confirm he has his glasses and that the prescription is current
options.rationale: An uncorrected visual deficit produces withdrawal and misunderstanding that look exactly like cognitive decline.

options.text: Review the medication list for ototoxic and anticholinergic drugs
options.rationale: Drugs are the first hypothesis for a new symptom in an older adult, not the last.

options.text: Assess for recent changes in his room, routine or roommate
options.rationale: An unstimulating or unfamiliar environment produces sensory deprivation, and deprivation produces withdrawal and disordered thinking.

options.text: Document the behavior change and reassess in one week
options.rationale: Documenting instead of acting. A week of untreated reversible deficit is a week of avoidable disability.

options.text: Explain to the family that this is an expected part of aging
options.rationale: A new change is never assumed to be age-related, and reassurance delivered before assessment is the most reliable wrong answer in this material.

questions.takeaway: Uncorrected sensory deficit imitates dementia and is reversible. Check the glasses, the hearing aid, the ear canal and the medication list before anyone writes the word confusion.
questions.strategy: Two options are comfortable and passive. Both of them accept the description instead of testing it.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Ears, eyes, drugs, environment.
Documentation follows the intervention, it does not replace it.
New is never normal aging.

elimination.verdict: A, B, C and D.

questions.stem: A nurse is preparing a hospital room for a patient who is newly blind. Which action best promotes safety?

options.text: Rearrange the furniture so the path to the bathroom is shortest
options.rationale: Well intentioned and dangerous. A blind patient navigates by a memorized layout, and moving furniture removes the map.

options.text: Orient the patient to the room and then leave everything where it is
options.rationale: Predictability is the safety intervention. Once the layout is learned, it has to stay constant, and anything moved gets announced.

options.text: Keep the room dimly lit to reduce glare and confusion
options.rationale: Light level is irrelevant to a patient with no usable vision and creates a hazard for everyone else in the room.

options.text: Use the call light to summon the patient rather than entering unannounced
options.rationale: The call light summons the nurse, not the patient. What matters is that staff identify themselves on entering and say when they leave.

questions.takeaway: For a visual deficit, safety is built out of consistency: a predictable layout, announced entries and exits, and nothing moved without telling the patient.
questions.strategy: Three options change something about the environment. The correct one is the only one that keeps it still.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.action: Ask what a blind patient navigates by
steps.detail: Memory of a fixed layout.
It erases the map.
Irrelevant to no usable vision.
It runs the wrong direction.

elimination.verdict: Orient once, then keep the room constant.

questions.stem: A patient who reads lips is admitted to a unit where staff wear masks. Which adaptation best preserves effective communication?

options.text: Speak more loudly through the mask so the words carry
options.rationale: Volume is not the problem. A mask removes the visual half of the message, and raising the pitch makes a high-frequency loss worse.

options.text: Use a clear-window mask or written communication, and confirm with teach-back
options.rationale: Restores the visual channel or replaces it, and teach-back is how you verify the message actually arrived rather than assuming a nod means understanding.

options.text: Ask a family member to relay all instructions by phone
options.rationale: Offloads the nurse's legal duty onto a third party and introduces a second chance for the message to be lost.

options.text: Shorten conversations to reduce the patient's frustration
options.rationale: Reduces the burden on the nurse and the information reaching the patient. Frustration is not the safety risk; missed information is.

questions.takeaway: Effective communication is a legal and ethical requirement. When the visual channel is removed, you restore it or replace it, and you verify with teach-back.
questions.strategy: One option is louder, one is shorter, one delegates. None of those puts the information back.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: The lips and the expression.
Shouting raises pitch into the lost range.
Both reduce the information the patient receives.

elimination.verdict: Restore the visual channel and confirm with teach-back. Nodding is not comprehension.

questions.scenario: A nurse rounds on four patients in different areas of the hospital.
questions.stem: For each patient, indicate whether the environment places them at risk for sensory deprivation or sensory overload.

rows.text: In protective isolation in a windowless room with no clock, television or visitors
rows.rationale: Isolation, no natural light, no time cues and nothing meaningful coming in. Every element of deprivation at once.

rows.text: Day three in intensive care with continuous alarms, hourly assessments and no protected sleep
rows.rationale: More input than the patient can sort, with no recovery period. This is the picture that produces agitation and pulling at lines.

rows.text: An older adult whose glasses and hearing aid were left at home on admission
rows.rationale: The stimulus is present and cannot reach the patient. An uncorrected deficit produces withdrawal and misunderstanding that imitate dementia.

rows.text: In the emergency department during a busy shift with bright lights and multiple caregivers asking questions
rows.rationale: Noise, light and several people competing for attention. Too much arriving at once to process.

questions.takeaway: Deprivation is too little meaningful input, or input the person cannot interpret. Overload is more than they can process. Both produce confusion, and both are reversible.
questions.strategy: The missing glasses row is the one students miss, because the environment is busy. Ask what is reaching the patient, not what is happening in the room.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Quiet and empty is deprivation.

steps.action: Ask how much can be processed
steps.detail: Alarms and interruptions with no rest is overload.
A busy room the patient cannot see or hear is still deprivation.

elimination.verdict: Two deprivation, two overload, and the deficit row is the trap.

questions.stem: A patient with expressive aphasia after a stroke becomes visibly frustrated trying to answer a question. What is the nurse's best response?

options.text: Finish the sentence for the patient to reduce the effort
options.rationale: Feels kind and takes the communication away. It also risks putting words in the patient's mouth that are not what they meant.

options.text: Allow time, ask questions that can be answered yes or no, and offer a communication board
options.rationale: Expressive aphasia means comprehension is intact and output is impaired. Time, closed questions and an alternative output channel all work with that.

options.text: Speak more slowly and loudly so the patient can understand
options.rationale: Treats it as a comprehension or hearing problem. In expressive aphasia the patient understands you perfectly, and volume implies otherwise.

options.text: Ask the family to interpret what the patient is trying to say
options.rationale: Bypasses the patient. Useful as a supplement, and not a substitute for communicating with the patient directly.

questions.takeaway: Expressive aphasia is an output problem with intact comprehension. Give time, use yes and no questions, and supply an alternative channel.
questions.strategy: Two options treat it as a hearing or comprehension problem. Two of them take the communication away from the patient.

strategies: Patient-centered option
Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Expressive: understanding intact, speech impaired.
That addresses comprehension, which is not affected.

steps.action: Cut finishing sentences and family interpreting
steps.detail: Both remove the patient from the exchange.

elimination.verdict: Time, closed questions and a communication board.

questions.stem: The nurse is teaching a community group about preventing sensory loss. Which statements are correct? Select all that apply.

options.text: Hearing and eye protection should be worn whenever there is occupational exposure
options.rationale: Noise-induced loss is the major preventable cause of sensory hearing loss, and protection before the exposure is the only thing that changes it.

options.text: Take a break every 20 minutes from close work and look at something 20 feet away for 20 seconds
options.rationale: The 20-20-20 rule. The distance is the active ingredient, because it is what relaxes the ciliary muscle.

options.text: Ultraviolet-blocking sunglasses reduce the risk of cataract
options.rationale: Chronic sun exposure is a named cataract risk, and blocking it is a cheap preventive measure.

options.text: Any hearing change after age 70 can reasonably be attributed to normal aging
options.rationale: Sudden or one-sided change is never aging. And while presbycusis is the most common age-related loss, impacted cerumen is the most common correctable cause, so a new change is assessed rather than attributed.

options.text: Cotton swabs are a safe way to keep the ear canal clear of wax
options.rationale: Swabs push wax deeper and are a named cause of canal trauma and external otitis.

options.text: Regular vision and hearing screening should continue at age-appropriate intervals through life
options.rationale: Screening frequency rises with age and with risk factors, and the nurse role is detection and referral.

questions.takeaway: Prevention is protection before exposure, screening at intervals, and never accepting a new change as age-related.
questions.strategy: The two wrong options are both things people believe. One reassures, one is a household habit.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.action: Keep the protective and screening statements
steps.detail: Protection, 20-20-20, sunglasses, screening.
Sudden or one-sided is never aging.
They impact the wax and injure the canal.

elimination.verdict: A, B, C and F.

questions.stem: A home health nurse visits a patient with moderate hearing loss and macular degeneration who lives alone. Which finding does the nurse address as the highest safety priority?

options.text: The patient has stopped attending a weekly social group
options.rationale: Social withdrawal is a real consequence of sensory loss and a quality of life concern. It is not what kills someone tonight.

options.text: The smoke alarm is a standard audible model with no visual alert
options.rationale: A patient who cannot hear the alarm has no warning of a fire. A flashing alert system is a safety intervention, not an accessory.

options.text: Medication bottles are labeled in standard-size print
options.rationale: A genuine problem with a straightforward fix, and it does not carry the same immediate lethality.

options.text: The patient reports the television is turned up very loud
options.rationale: A finding that confirms the hearing loss rather than a hazard in itself.

questions.takeaway: Hearing loss is a safety problem before it is a communication problem. A client who cannot hear the alarm is in danger in a way that has nothing to do with conversation.
questions.strategy: Every option is a real finding. Rank them by what happens if nothing is done.

strategies: Priority key word
Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Only one option involves a fire.

steps.action: Cut the withdrawal and the television
steps.detail: Both are consequences, not hazards.
Important, fixable, and not immediately dangerous.

elimination.verdict: The smoke alarm. Visual alerting devices belong in discharge teaching.

questions.stem: Which statement by a nursing student about sensory alterations requires correction?

options.text: "Sensory deprivation and sensory overload can both cause disorientation."
options.rationale: Accurate. Both ends of the spectrum produce confusion, which is why the environment has to be assessed in either direction.

options.text: "An older adult who seems confused should be screened for a correctable sensory deficit."
options.rationale: Accurate, and it is the most commonly missed assessment in this material.

options.text: "Once a patient has adapted to a constant stimulus, they stop noticing it."
options.rationale: Accurate. That is sensory adaptation, and it is why a patient stops hearing a monitor that still alarms.

options.text: "A patient who has hallucinations in the hospital is showing early dementia."
options.rationale: This is the statement to correct. Hallucinations are a documented finding in sensory deprivation and in delirium, both of which are reversible, and assuming dementia closes off the assessment that would find the cause.

questions.takeaway: Hallucinations and disordered thinking appear in sensory deprivation and delirium long before they mean dementia. The reversible explanation is ruled out first.
questions.strategy: Negative polarity: you are hunting the false statement, so read each option asking whether it is true rather than whether it sounds good.

strategies: Negative polarity
Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Find the one that is wrong.
Both extremes confuse, deficits imitate dementia, adaptation is real.
Hallucinations belong to deprivation and delirium first.

elimination.verdict: The dementia statement. It skips the reversible causes.

questions.stem: A patient receiving furosemide has a serum potassium of 2.8 mEq/L. Which assessment finding does the nurse report immediately?

options.text: Constipation and abdominal distention
options.rationale: A real finding in hypokalemia and not the one that kills. Smooth muscle slows along with everything else.

options.text: Shallow respirations with a weak cough
options.rationale: Hypokalemia weakens every muscle including the diaphragm and the intercostals. Respiratory muscle weakness is the finding that turns a laboratory value into an emergency.

options.text: Generalized fatigue and leg weakness
options.rationale: Expected and important, and it is the background against which you look for the breathing.

options.text: Prominent U waves on the cardiac monitor
options.rationale: The classic electrocardiogram change in hypokalemia, and it belongs in the report. It is still not the finding that takes priority over ventilation.

questions.takeaway: Weakness is a respiratory finding until you rule it out. Hypokalemia, hypermagnesemia and hyponatremia all weaken the muscles that breathe.
questions.strategy: Every option is a genuine finding in hypokalemia. The question is which one threatens the airway and breathing.

strategies: Apply the ABCs
Priority key word
Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Only one option is about breathing.

steps.action: Note that U waves are tempting
steps.detail: They are the textbook sign, which is exactly why they are offered.

steps.action: Cut the gut and the fatigue
steps.detail: Both are expected and neither is immediately dangerous.

elimination.verdict: Shallow respirations. Assess the breathing, not just the grip.

questions.stem: A patient with chronic kidney disease has a serum potassium of 7.1 mEq/L with peaked T waves. The prescriber orders IV calcium gluconate. The patient asks what it will do. What is the nurse's best response?

options.text: It will lower your potassium level quickly
options.rationale: The single most reliable near-miss distractor in this chapter. Calcium does not change the potassium at all.

options.text: It will protect your heart while we work on lowering the potassium
options.rationale: Calcium raises the threshold potential of cardiac cells, which stabilizes the membrane against the arrhythmia. It buys time and treats nothing.

options.text: It will help your kidneys excrete the extra potassium
options.rationale: Excretion is what a cation exchange resin or dialysis does. Calcium has no role in elimination.

options.text: It will move the potassium into your cells for storage
options.rationale: That is insulin with dextrose, or a beta agonist. Those shift potassium; calcium does not.

questions.takeaway: IV calcium in hyperkalemia protects the heart and changes the level not at all. Shifting is insulin and dextrose; removing is a resin or dialysis.
questions.strategy: Three options describe real hyperkalemia treatments. Only one of them is what calcium actually does.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Stabilize, shift, remove. Three different jobs.
It stabilizes.
Lowering, excreting and shifting all belong to other drugs.

elimination.verdict: Cardiac protection while another drug does the lowering.

questions.stem: A patient has been receiving potassium replacement for two days and the serum potassium remains 3.0 mEq/L. Which laboratory value does the nurse check next?

options.text: Serum magnesium
options.rationale: Low magnesium makes the kidney waste potassium and blocks it from staying in the cell. Potassium will not come up while the magnesium is low, no matter how much you give.

options.text: Serum albumin
options.rationale: Albumin matters for interpreting a calcium level, not a potassium one.

options.text: Serum phosphorus
options.rationale: Phosphorus moves inversely with calcium. It has no direct role in potassium replacement failing.

options.text: Serum chloride
options.rationale: Chloride tracks sodium and acid-base status. It does not explain refractory hypokalemia.

questions.takeaway: When a level will not respond to correction, the first question is which related electrolyte nobody checked. Potassium will not correct while magnesium is low.
questions.strategy: The stem is not asking about hypokalemia. It is asking why a correct treatment is not working.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Two days of replacement with no movement.
Magnesium, every time.
Albumin and phosphorus belong to a different pairing.

elimination.verdict: Magnesium. Read labs as a set, not one line at a time.

questions.stem: A patient with hypocalcemia has a total calcium of 7.6 mg/dL. Which findings does the nurse expect? Select all that apply.

options.text: Positive Trousseau sign when the blood pressure cuff is inflated
options.rationale: Carpal spasm with cuff inflation. Low calcium lowers the threshold at which nerves fire, so ischemia provokes a spasm.

options.text: Tingling and numbness around the mouth and in the fingertips
options.rationale: Paresthesia is usually the earliest complaint and it is the one patients report themselves.

options.text: Hyperactive deep tendon reflexes
options.rationale: Nerve and muscle are overexcitable, so reflexes are brisk.

options.text: Prolonged QT interval on the electrocardiogram
options.rationale: Low calcium lengthens the plateau phase of repolarization, which shows as a long QT and carries a risk of torsades de pointes.

options.text: Deep bone pain with kidney stones
options.rationale: That is hypercalcemia. Calcium coming out of bone into urine is a high-calcium picture.

options.text: Constipation and decreased bowel sounds
options.rationale: Also hypercalcemia. Low calcium makes smooth muscle overactive, giving cramping and diarrhea instead.

questions.takeaway: Low calcium excites nerve and muscle: tetany, tingling, brisk reflexes, positive Trousseau and Chvostek, and a prolonged QT. High calcium sedates them.
questions.strategy: Two options belong to the opposite imbalance. Ask of each one whether it sounds excitable or sluggish.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Low calcium excites, high calcium sedates.
Spasm, tingling, brisk reflexes, long QT.

steps.action: Cut stones, bone pain and constipation
steps.detail: All three are the sluggish, high-calcium picture.

elimination.verdict: A, B, C and D.

questions.stem: A patient with cirrhosis has a serum sodium of 124 mEq/L, ascites, 3+ pitting edema and a weight gain of 4 kg this week. Which intervention does the nurse anticipate?

options.text: Infusion of 0.9% sodium chloride at 150 mL/hr
options.rationale: Saline into a fluid-overloaded hyponatremic patient makes both problems worse. The sodium is low because there is too much water, not too little salt.

options.text: Fluid restriction with daily weights
options.rationale: This is dilutional hyponatremia. The sodium is diluted by retained water, so removing water is what raises the number.

options.text: Encouraging salty broths and adding salt to meals
options.rationale: Adds sodium to a patient who is already retaining water and will retain more with it.

options.text: Rapid infusion of 3% sodium chloride over two hours
options.rationale: Hypertonic saline is reserved for severe symptomatic hyponatremia with seizures or coma, given slowly and with close monitoring. Correcting fast causes osmotic demyelination.

questions.takeaway: Find the volume status before you treat the sodium. A low sodium with edema and weight gain is too much water, and the treatment is restriction rather than replacement.
questions.strategy: Two options add sodium and one adds volume. The edema and the weight gain tell you which direction the patient needs to move.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Ascites, 3+ edema and 4 kg of gain.
Adding fluid to an overloaded patient.
Sodium follows water in, and there is already too much water.

elimination.verdict: Fluid restriction. Hyponatremia is not automatically a sodium deficiency.

questions.stem: A patient receiving magnesium sulfate for preeclampsia becomes drowsy, and the nurse finds absent patellar reflexes with a respiratory rate of 10. What does the nurse do first?

options.text: Stop the magnesium infusion
options.rationale: Reflexes go first, then respirations, then rhythm. The progression has already reached breathing, and the first action is to stop what is causing it.

options.text: Administer calcium gluconate as the antidote
options.rationale: Calcium is the antidote and it comes after stopping the infusion. Giving the antidote while the drug keeps running is treating around the cause.

options.text: Notify the prescriber of the assessment findings
options.rationale: Necessary and not first. Notification follows the action that stops the harm.

options.text: Place the patient on continuous pulse oximetry
options.rationale: Monitoring a patient who is being poisoned does not stop the poisoning.

questions.takeaway: Hypermagnesemia progresses reflexes, then respirations, then rhythm. Checking the patellar reflex before each hour of infusion is how you catch it before the breathing.
questions.strategy: Three of the four options are correct actions and only one of them removes the cause.

strategies: Priority key word
Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Stop before you call.

steps.action: Note that the antidote is tempting
steps.detail: It is right and it is second.
Both follow the intervention.

elimination.verdict: Stop the infusion, then calcium gluconate, then notify.

questions.stem: A patient has a total calcium of 7.8 mg/dL with a serum albumin of 2.1 g/dL. The patient has no tingling, no spasm and a normal QT interval. How does the nurse interpret this?

options.text: The patient has significant hypocalcemia and needs replacement now
options.rationale: Treating the number instead of the patient. Nothing in the assessment supports a functional deficit.

options.text: The low albumin has lowered the total calcium without lowering the active calcium
options.rationale: Roughly half of serum calcium travels bound to albumin. Less albumin means less bound calcium and a lower total, while the ionized fraction that actually does the work is unchanged.

options.text: The result is a laboratory error and should be redrawn
options.rationale: The two values are consistent with each other, which is the opposite of an error.

options.text: The patient is developing hyperparathyroidism
options.rationale: That raises calcium rather than lowering it.

questions.takeaway: Low albumin lowers the total calcium without lowering the calcium that is working. Check the albumin, or ask for the ionized calcium, before treating a number.
questions.strategy: The absence of symptoms is the finding the question is built on. A truly low ionized calcium would show itself.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Calcium is reported with albumin for a reason.
No tingling, no spasm, normal QT.
Nothing functional is wrong.

elimination.verdict: A dilutional artifact of low albumin. Ask for an ionized calcium.

questions.stem: A nurse is caring for a patient with a serum sodium of 158 mEq/L after prolonged fever and poor intake. Which nursing actions are appropriate? Select all that apply.

options.text: Monitor level of consciousness at least every four hours
options.rationale: Hypernatremia pulls water out of brain cells. Neurologic change is the earliest and most important finding.

options.text: Anticipate a hypotonic intravenous solution prescribed to run slowly
options.rationale: The water deficit is replaced gradually. Correcting a high sodium too quickly pulls water into brain cells and causes cerebral edema.

options.text: Institute seizure precautions
options.rationale: Both extremes of sodium change brain cell volume and both can produce seizures.

options.text: Offer oral fluids on a schedule rather than waiting for the patient to ask
options.rationale: Thirst is blunted in older adults and unreliable as a guide. A schedule works where waiting does not.

options.text: Correct the sodium to normal within the first eight hours
options.rationale: Rapid correction in either direction causes harm. Down too fast swells the brain; up too fast damages myelin.

options.text: Restrict free water until the sodium normalizes
options.rationale: This patient is short of water, not carrying too much. Restriction would worsen it.

questions.takeaway: Both sodium extremes are brain problems, and both are corrected slowly. Fast down causes cerebral edema; fast up causes osmotic demyelination.
questions.strategy: Two options are written to sound decisive. Speed is the trap in every sodium question.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: A high sodium here means a water deficit.
Monitoring, seizure precautions, scheduled fluids.
Rapid correction is never the right option.
Wrong direction for a water deficit.

elimination.verdict: A, B, C and D.

questions.stem: Two hours after an intravenous infusion was started, a patient reports that the site feels tight. The nurse finds the area around the catheter cool, pale and swollen, with the swelling spreading outward from the insertion point. What does the nurse do?

options.text: Apply warm compresses and continue the infusion at a slower rate
options.rationale: Warmth is for phlebitis. Continuing any rate keeps pushing solution into tissue.

options.text: Stop the infusion, remove the catheter and elevate the extremity
options.rationale: Cool, pale, swollen and spreading is infiltration. Stop, remove, elevate, and do not compress.

options.text: Massage the area to disperse the fluid and reduce the swelling
options.rationale: Massage forces more solution into the tissue and can worsen the injury.

options.text: Aspirate from the catheter and flush with 10 mL of normal saline to confirm patency
options.rationale: A flush adds volume to tissue that already has too much, and patency is not the question. A catheter can flush perfectly while it sits outside the vein.

questions.takeaway: Infiltration runs cool and spreads around the site. Phlebitis runs warm and follows the vein. A streak or a palpable cord is always phlebitis.
questions.strategy: The temperature and the direction of spread are the two cues that separate the two complications, and the stem gives you both.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: That rules out phlebitis and infection.
Not along the vein, so not a cord.
Both belong to the other diagnosis or make this one worse.
Patency is not safety.

elimination.verdict: Infiltration. Stop, remove, elevate, and do not compress.

questions.scenario: A nurse reviews four patients on a medical unit, each with one abnormal electrolyte.
questions.stem: For each finding, indicate whether it reflects an overexcitable state or a slowed state.

rows.text: Serum calcium 7.4 mg/dL with carpal spasm and a prolonged QT
rows.rationale: Hypocalcemia. Less calcium at the membrane means nerves fire more easily, so you get tetany.

rows.text: Serum magnesium 4.8 mEq/L with facial flushing and absent deep tendon reflexes
rows.rationale: Hypermagnesemia. Magnesium blocks neuromuscular transmission, so reflexes go first, then respirations, then rhythm.

rows.text: Serum potassium 6.4 mEq/L with tall peaked T waves and abdominal cramping
rows.rationale: Hyperkalemia. The resting membrane sits closer to threshold, so cardiac and smooth muscle are irritable.

rows.text: Serum calcium 12.6 mg/dL with lethargy, constipation and diminished reflexes
rows.rationale: Hypercalcemia. Extra calcium at the membrane raises the threshold, so everything is harder to fire.

questions.takeaway: Calcium and magnesium sedate the membrane, so low means excitable and high means slowed. Potassium is the opposite: high means excitable.
questions.strategy: Potassium inverts the pattern, which is why it is placed third. Sort calcium and magnesium by the rule, then handle potassium separately.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.action: Apply the calcium and magnesium rule
steps.detail: Low excites, high sedates.
High potassium excites, low potassium weakens.

steps.action: Check the findings against the label
steps.detail: Spasm and peaked T waves are excitement. Absent reflexes, lethargy and constipation are slowing.

elimination.verdict: Two overexcitable, two slowed, and potassium is the one that breaks the pattern.

questions.stem: A patient with cerebral edema after a closed head injury has a serum sodium of 118 mEq/L and is becoming drowsy. Which IV solution does the nurse anticipate?

options.text: 3% sodium chloride
options.rationale: A hypertonic solution has a higher osmolarity than plasma, so it pulls water out of cells and into the bloodstream. Severe hyponatremia and cerebral edema are both listed indications for hypertonic saline, and pulling water into the vasculature lowers intracranial pressure while raising the sodium.

options.text: 0.45% sodium chloride
options.rationale: A hypotonic solution is more dilute than plasma, so water shifts into cells and they swell. This is the option that looks right because it is saline.

options.text: 0.9% sodium chloride
options.rationale: An isotonic solution matches plasma osmolarity, so there is no net water movement across cell membranes. It expands volume, which is a different problem from the one in the stem.

options.text: 5% dextrose in water
options.rationale: D5W is isotonic in the bag and becomes hypotonic once the dextrose is metabolized, leaving free water. This is among the worst choices here despite appearing on the isotonic list.

questions.takeaway: Hypertonic solutions pull water out of cells. That single action is why the same fluid treats severe hyponatremia and cerebral edema at once.

questions.stem: A patient with diabetic ketoacidosis has completed initial fluid resuscitation with 0.9% sodium chloride and is now hemodynamically stable with a blood pressure of 118 over 70. Which solution does the nurse anticipate for continued maintenance fluid?

options.text: 3% sodium chloride
options.rationale: Hypertonic saline pulls water out of cells into the vasculature and is reserved for severe hyponatremia and cerebral edema. The osmotic diuresis of ketoacidosis has already dehydrated the cells, so pulling more water out would worsen the deficit.

options.text: 0.45% sodium chloride
options.rationale: Half normal saline is hypotonic, so water shifts into cells by osmosis and rehydrates them. Diabetic ketoacidosis after initial resuscitation is a named indication for hypotonic fluid, because the vascular space has been filled and the cellular dehydration remains.

options.text: 10% dextrose in water
options.rationale: D10W is hypertonic and is used for hypoglycemia. Adding concentrated dextrose at this stage works against the treatment, and dextrose is added later only once glucose falls to a target.

options.text: Lactated Ringer's
options.rationale: Lactated Ringer's is isotonic and produces no net water shift across cell membranes. Continuing it maintains volume without addressing the cellular dehydration that remains.

questions.takeaway: Hypotonic fluids move water into cells, which is why they follow rather than lead resuscitation in ketoacidosis. Fill the vascular space first, then rehydrate the cells.

questions.stem: A nursing student asks why 5% dextrose in water is not used to resuscitate a patient in hemorrhagic shock even though it appears on the isotonic list. Which response is correct?

options.text: It contains too much dextrose and will cause the blood to clot in the tubing
options.rationale: Clotting in the line is a concern with lactated Ringer's during a transfusion because it contains calcium. That is a transfusion rule, not the reason it fails as a resuscitation fluid.

options.text: It is hypertonic and would pull fluid out of the cells the patient needs to hydrate
options.rationale: Hypertonic solutions have osmolarity above plasma and shrink cells. This option has the direction and the classification both reversed.

options.text: It is isotonic in the bag, and once the dextrose is metabolized the remaining free water moves into cells
options.rationale: Tonicity describes the solution compared with plasma at the moment of infusion. The dextrose is taken up and metabolized, leaving water that behaves hypotonically and shifts into cells rather than staying in the vasculature where volume is needed.

options.text: It raises blood glucose, which is the only reason it is avoided in trauma
options.rationale: Dextrose does raise serum glucose, and that matters in some patients. The absolute word 'only' also signals a wrong option, because it rules out the actual mechanism.

questions.takeaway: A solution's tonicity can change once it is in the body. D5W is the standing example, which is why it appears on the isotonic list and is still not a volume expander.

questions.stem: A patient has lost an estimated 1200 mL of blood during surgery and has a blood pressure of 88 over 52 with a pulse of 118. While blood is being crossmatched, which solution does the nurse expect to infuse?

options.text: 10% dextrose in water
options.rationale: D10W is hypertonic and is used for hypoglycemia and for expanding intravascular volume. It also carries risks of cell dehydration and hypernatremia that are unnecessary when an isotonic fluid will do the job.

options.text: 0.45% sodium chloride
options.rationale: Half normal saline is hypotonic, so most of the infused water leaves the vasculature and enters cells. A fluid that moves water out of that space is the opposite of what is needed.

options.text: 3% sodium chloride
options.rationale: Hypertonic saline does expand intravascular volume by pulling water out of cells, and it is reserved for severe hyponatremia and cerebral edema. Using it here treats the volume at the cost of dehydrating cells for no reason.

options.text: Lactated Ringer's
options.rationale: Lactated Ringer's is isotonic at 273 mOsm/L, so infused volume stays in the extracellular space and expands circulating volume without shifting water into or out of cells. Volume expansion and hemorrhage resuscitation are the listed uses for isotonic fluids.

questions.takeaway: Hemorrhage empties the vascular compartment, so the fluid that fixes it is the one that stays there. That is the definition of isotonic.

questions.stem: A nurse is preparing to transfuse a unit of packed red blood cells. Which actions are required before the infusion begins? Select all that apply.

options.text: Warm the unit to room temperature on the counter for 30 minutes
options.rationale: Packed red cells are stored between 1 and 6 degrees Celsius and must be infused within 4 hours of issue. Blood warming, when indicated, is done with a dedicated device.

options.text: Have two licensed nurses independently verify the product label against the identification band, ABO and Rh type, unit number, and expiration date
options.rationale: Independent double verification means two qualified people check separately and both sign. Incompatible transfusion is a sentinel event, and this check is what prevents it.

options.text: Establish or confirm an 18 to 20 gauge intravenous access
options.rationale: Gauge describes lumen width, and a wider lumen allows red cells through without excessive resistance. Eighteen to twenty gauge is the stated requirement for blood, and 18 gauge is preferred for blood products specifically.

options.text: Record a full set of baseline vital signs
options.rationale: Baseline vital signs are the values recorded before the infusion starts. Temperature, pulse, respirations, blood pressure, and oxygen saturation are recorded before the unit is started, rechecked at 15 minutes, then every 30 to 60 minutes.

options.text: Confirm that signed informed consent is on file
options.rationale: Informed consent is the patient's documented agreement after being told purpose, benefits, risks, and alternatives. Before the product is retrieved from the blood bank, because the unit's clock and cold chain start the moment it leaves.

options.text: Prime the administration set with 5% dextrose in water
options.rationale: Priming fills the tubing with fluid before connecting it. Dextrose causes red cells to clump and hemolyze, so this action would damage the product being given.

questions.takeaway: The pre-transfusion checks all exist to prevent one event: giving the wrong blood to the wrong patient. Consent, two-nurse verification, adequate access, and baseline vitals.

questions.stem: Two nurses are verifying a unit of blood at the bedside. One nurse reads aloud from the blood bank record while the other listens and agrees. Which statement about this process is correct?

options.text: The process is incorrect, because each nurse must verify the information independently
options.rationale: Independent verification means each nurse checks the source documents and the patient separately and then compares conclusions. The second set of eyes exists to catch the first nurse's error, and it cannot do that if it never looks.

options.text: The verification is complete once both nurses sign the transfusion record
options.rationale: Signing documents that verification occurred. The signature records the process; it does not substitute for it, and both nurses signing a flawed check simply records the flaw twice.

options.text: The process is acceptable as long as one of the two nurses is the nurse who will start the infusion
options.rationale: Which nurse hangs the unit does not change how the check was performed. This adds a true-sounding condition that is irrelevant to the flaw.

options.text: The process is acceptable if the patient states their own name and date of birth
options.rationale: Patient participation in identification is genuinely good practice and confirms one element. Those are the other required elements, and they are checked against documents rather than against the patient's memory.

questions.takeaway: Two-nurse verification means two independent checks, not one check with a witness. The second nurse exists to catch what the first missed.

questions.stem: A unit of packed red blood cells was started 10 minutes ago. The nurse is planning the monitoring schedule for this transfusion. When does the nurse plan the first reassessment of vital signs after initiation?

options.text: At 30 minutes after the start
options.rationale: Every 30 to 60 minutes is the correct interval for the remainder of the transfusion. This is the right number in the wrong position, which makes it the closest wrong answer.

options.text: At 15 minutes after the start
options.rationale: Reassessment at 15 minutes is the scheduled early check after a baseline set. After it, vital signs are taken every 30 to 60 minutes and again at completion.

options.text: At 60 minutes after the start
options.rationale: Sixty minutes is the outer limit of the ongoing interval once the transfusion is established. A substantial part of the unit, which is precisely what the early check is designed to avoid.

options.text: At the halfway point of the unit
options.rationale: Monitoring is scheduled by clock time rather than by volume infused. Rates vary between patients, so a volume-based schedule would place the check at unpredictable times.

questions.takeaway: Baseline, then 15 minutes, then every 30 to 60 minutes, then completion. The 15-minute check exists because early reactions happen in the first small volume.

questions.stem: A patient receiving lactated Ringer's through the only IV site is scheduled for a transfusion. Which action does the nurse take before hanging the blood?

options.text: Flush the existing line with lactated Ringer's and connect the blood to the same tubing
options.rationale: Lactated Ringer's contains calcium. Flushing with it leaves the incompatible fluid in contact with the product.

options.text: Add 5% dextrose in water to the line to keep it open during the transfusion
options.rationale: Dextrose causes red cells to clump and hemolyze on contact. Only 0.9% sodium chloride may contact blood products.

options.text: Change the solution to 0.9% sodium chloride with new tubing before connecting the blood
options.rationale: Normal saline is the only solution permitted with blood products, and new tubing ensures no residual incompatible fluid remains. Isotonic saline is also what flushes before and after the unit.

options.text: Run the blood alongside the lactated Ringer's through a Y connector
options.rationale: A Y connector allows two solutions to meet before entering the vein. The incompatibility is with the blood itself, not with the bag it hangs beside.

questions.takeaway: Only 0.9% sodium chloride touches blood. Dextrose hemolyzes red cells and the calcium in lactated Ringer's clots them.

questions.stem: A patient needs two units of packed red blood cells. The existing peripheral access is a 24 gauge catheter in the dorsal hand. Which action does the nurse take?

options.text: Use the existing 24 gauge catheter and infuse each unit slowly over 6 hours
options.rationale: Slowing an infusion reduces resistance. This option breaks a second rule to work around the first.

options.text: Use the existing 24 gauge catheter with a pressure bag to overcome the resistance
options.rationale: A pressure bag forces fluid through at a higher driving pressure. Hemolysis, which destroys the product being given and releases its contents into the patient.

options.text: Establish new access with a 22 gauge catheter in the dorsal hand
options.rationale: Twenty-two gauge is a small-bore size recommended for pediatric, elderly, and fragile veins. Dorsal hand veins are also the sites to avoid in older patients and are a poor choice for a viscous product.

options.text: Establish new access with an 18 gauge catheter in a forearm vein
options.rationale: Gauge describes lumen width, and smaller numbers mean wider lumens. A 24 gauge catheter is a small-bore size intended for fragile veins and maintenance fluids.

questions.takeaway: Blood needs 18 to 20 gauge access, with 18 gauge preferred. Working around an inadequate catheter with time or pressure breaks a different rule each time.

questions.stem: A patient scheduled for long-term antibiotic therapy had a left mastectomy with axillary node dissection two years ago and has an arteriovenous fistula in the right forearm for dialysis. Where does the nurse plan vascular access?

options.text: Consultation for a central vascular access device
options.rationale: When both upper extremities are contraindicated and the therapy is long-term, the peripheral options are exhausted rather than merely inconvenient. With a mastectomy limb on one side and a fistula limb on the other, central access is the plan rather than a fallback.
