options.rationale: Level 4 requires passing the walk test, which checks standing balance and gait by having the patient march in place and advance a foot. You cannot skip a failed test to reach a higher level.

questions.takeaway: The tool is a sequence of four tests, and the level is named by the first test the patient cannot complete. Sit and shake, stretch and point, stand, walk.

questions.stem: A patient has completed the sitting and lower-extremity portions of the Bedside Mobility Assessment Tool successfully. Before asking the patient to rise toward standing, which factor does the nurse evaluate?

options.text: Whether an assistive device is available at the bedside
options.rationale: An assistive device is equipment such as a walker or cane that supports weight and balance. Having one ready is sensible and is not the evaluation specified before this test, which makes this the closest wrong answer.

options.text: The patient's cognition, orientation, and whether delirium is present
options.rationale: Delirium is an acute, fluctuating confusion with a physical cause. Standing is the point where the assessment first puts the patient's weight on their own legs, so mental status is checked before it rather than after.

options.text: The patient's grip strength in both hands
options.rationale: Grip strength measures hand and forearm function. Grip was already sampled during the handshake in the first test, and it says nothing about the legs.

options.text: Whether the patient reached across midline during the earlier step
options.rationale: Reaching across midline demonstrates trunk control and seated balance. It is accurate information that has already done its work.

questions.takeaway: Strength and judgment are separate systems and fail separately. A patient whose legs work and whose thinking does not will stand up and go down.

questions.stem: A patient has left-sided weakness after a stroke. The patient can raise the left arm about halfway toward shoulder height and then cannot lift it any further. Which exercise does the nurse use to maintain shoulder mobility?

options.text: Passive range of motion, with the nurse moving the arm through the whole arc
options.rationale: Passive range of motion means someone else moves the joint while the patient's muscle does nothing. Taking over the whole arc wastes the muscle activity the patient still has, and passive work maintains flexibility without building strength.

options.text: Active range of motion, with the patient raising the arm through the full arc unaided
options.rationale: Active range of motion means the patient performs the entire movement alone. The joint would never reach full range, and stiffness would develop in the part that is never used.

options.text: Active-assistive range of motion, with the patient raising the arm as far as possible and the nurse completing the movement
options.rationale: Active-assistive range of motion means the patient moves the joint as far as they can and the nurse supplies the remainder. The muscle works through the portion the patient controls, which preserves strength, and the joint still reaches full range, which preserves flexibility.

options.text: Isometric exercise, with the patient tightening the shoulder muscles without moving the joint
options.rationale: Isometric exercise contracts the muscle without moving the joint. Isometric work builds static strength and joint stability and does nothing for range.

questions.takeaway: Whenever a patient can contribute any part of a movement, they do that part. Active-assistive is the choice that keeps muscle working and still carries the joint through full range.

questions.stem: A patient has a long arm cast after a forearm fracture and will wear it for six weeks. The patient asks how to avoid losing strength in that arm. Which exercise does the nurse teach?

options.text: Move the elbow and wrist through their full range several times daily
options.rationale: Range of motion carries a joint through its arc. Joints above and below a cast are exercised where they are free, and the joints inside it are immobilized on purpose while the bone heals.

options.text: Lift a light hand weight with the casted arm
options.rationale: Lifting a weight through an arc is isotonic exercise, in which the muscle contracts while the joint moves. This is the correct exercise for building dynamic strength and the wrong one for a limb that must stay still.

options.text: Rest the arm completely until the cast is removed
options.rationale: Complete rest means no muscle activity at all. Resting sounds protective and guarantees the outcome the patient asked how to avoid.

options.text: Tighten and release the muscles inside the cast without moving the joints
options.rationale: Isometric exercise contracts the muscle without joint movement. It increases static strength and builds joint stability, and it can be used safely around painful or healing tissue, so the muscle keeps working for the six weeks the joint cannot.

questions.takeaway: Isometric exercise is the answer when a joint must not move. The muscle can still be loaded, so strength and joint stability survive the period of immobilization.

questions.stem: A patient walks the length of the hallway with a nurse. Which findings indicate that the patient exceeded activity tolerance? Select all that apply.

options.text: The patient becomes light-headed and reaches for the handrail
options.rationale: Dizziness is a listed tolerance parameter and it signals that perfusion to the brain has dropped. A patient who needs the handrail to stay upright is at the point where the activity becomes a fall.

options.text: Heart rate remains 118 ten minutes after returning to the chair
options.rationale: Recovery is the last item on the list of things to evaluate and the one most often skipped. A sustained elevation says the patient did more than the cardiovascular system could absorb, even if the walk itself looked acceptable.

options.text: Heart rate rises from 78 to 92 during the walk and returns to 80 within two minutes of sitting
options.rationale: Activity tolerance is judged by the response to activity and by the recovery afterward. This is the body working correctly, not failing.

options.text: Oxygen saturation falls from 96 percent to 87 percent during the walk
options.rationale: Oxygen saturation measures how much of the hemoglobin is carrying oxygen. Oxygenation is one of the listed tolerance parameters, and a drop of nine points into the eighties means demand has outrun the patient's ability to supply it.

options.text: The patient stops twice and says it is hard to catch a breath
options.rationale: Dyspnea is the subjective sense of not getting enough air. Having to stop is the functional version of the same finding.

options.text: Respiratory rate rises from 16 to 20 and settles back to 16 after three minutes
options.rationale: Respiratory rate is one of the tolerance parameters. A modest increase during walking that resolves on sitting is the expected response.

questions.takeaway: Activity tolerance is heart rate, respiratory rate, oxygenation, dyspnea, fatigue, pain, dizziness, and the ability to recover afterward. Rises during exertion are expected; what matters is how large they are and whether they resolve.

questions.stem: A nurse performs a neurovascular assessment on a patient six hours after surgical repair of an ankle fracture. Which finding does the nurse report to the provider immediately?

options.text: Capillary refill of four seconds in the toes with new numbness of the foot, compared with two seconds and normal sensation on the other side
options.rationale: Capillary refill is the time for color to return after pressure on the nail bed, normally under three seconds, and numbness is loss of sensation. Absent or diminished pulses, a cool or pale extremity, new numbness, and sudden loss of movement are all findings to report.

options.text: Moderate swelling at the surgical site
options.rationale: Swelling is fluid accumulating in injured tissue. What would concern you is swelling that is rapid or increasing quickly, and the stem describes neither.

options.text: Bruising visible along the lateral ankle
options.rationale: Bruising is blood that has escaped into the tissue from the injury and the surgery. It is an expected finding after a fracture and its repair.

options.text: Pain rated 5 of 10 that decreases after the ordered analgesic
options.rationale: Pain is one of the neurovascular parameters. This pain responded to the ordered dose, which is the reassuring version of the finding.

questions.takeaway: Neurovascular assessment is color, temperature, capillary refill, pulses, sensation, movement, and pain, and it is always compared side to side. Two abnormal findings in the same limb with a normal opposite side is the pattern that gets reported.

questions.stem: A patient has been immobile in bed for two weeks following a spinal cord injury. The nurse finds that both feet rest with the toes pointed downward and the ankles can no longer be brought to a neutral position. Which complication has developed?

options.text: Bone demineralization
options.rationale: Bone demineralization is the loss of mineral from bone that is not being loaded. It shows on imaging or in calcium studies, not as a joint that will not move.

options.text: Foot drop, which is a plantar flexion contracture
options.rationale: A contracture is the permanent shortening of muscle and tendon that limits joint mobility, and plantar flexion is the toes-pointed position of the ankle. That is foot drop, and it is prevented by maintaining neutral alignment, performing range of motion, and using supportive devices.

options.text: Muscle atrophy
options.rationale: Atrophy is the shrinking of muscle that is not being used. This patient almost certainly has atrophy too, and atrophy does not lock a joint in a fixed position, which is what the stem describes.

options.text: Venous stasis
options.rationale: Venous stasis is blood pooling in the legs because the muscle pump has stopped working. It raises the risk of thrombus formation and presents as swelling or as a clot, not as a rigid ankle.

questions.takeaway: Contractures are permanent shortening, so prevention is the whole intervention. Range of motion, neutral alignment, and supportive devices are scheduled rather than offered when there is time.

questions.stem: A patient is on bed rest after spinal surgery. The nurse hears diminished breath sounds at both lung bases with no adventitious sounds, notes that the patient's cough is weak, and finds that the oxygen saturation has fallen from 97 to 92 percent. The temperature is 36.8 C. Which complication is developing?

options.text: Pneumonia
options.rationale: Pneumonia is infection of the lung tissue. It has not yet.

options.text: Thrombus formation in the legs
options.rationale: A thrombus is a clot forming in a vein where blood has stopped moving. Thrombus is a genuine risk for this patient and is not what these findings describe.

options.text: Atelectasis
options.rationale: Atelectasis is the collapse of small airways and alveoli that are not being inflated. Diminished sounds without adventitious sounds means air is not reaching the area rather than moving through something.

options.text: Negative nitrogen balance
options.rationale: Negative nitrogen balance means the body is breaking down more protein than it takes in. It is a metabolic effect of immobility, not a respiratory one.

questions.takeaway: Flat positioning reduces lung expansion, a weak cough leaves secretions in place, and the dependent bases collapse first. Atelectasis is the step before pneumonia, not the same thing.

questions.stem: A patient has been on prolonged bed rest. For each nursing action, indicate the complication of immobility it is intended to prevent.

rows.text: Sits the patient upright and has the patient cough and deep breathe every two hours
rows.rationale: Atelectasis is the collapse of alveoli that are not being inflated. Lung expansion and the movement of retained secretions, which are the two things that fail when a patient stays flat.

rows.text: Applies sequential compression devices and has the patient perform leg exercises
rows.rationale: Venous stasis is blood pooling in the legs once the muscle pump stops working. Movement of blood out of the legs, which is what prevents a clot from forming.

rows.text: Takes every joint through its full arc twice daily
rows.rationale: A contracture is permanent shortening of muscle and tendon that limits joint mobility. Range of motion is the direct prevention.

rows.text: Repositions the patient on a schedule and lifts rather than drags during the move
rows.rationale: Pressure, friction, and shear are the three mechanical forces that injure skin, and all three reduce circulation to the tissue. The schedule limits time under pressure, and lifting instead of dragging removes friction and shear.

rows.text: Raises the head of the bed in stages and has the patient sit at the edge of the bed before standing
rows.rationale: Orthostatic hypotension is a fall in blood pressure when the patient moves upright, so the brain briefly goes short. Time for the circulation to adjust before the patient takes weight, which is why gradual position changes are the listed prevention.

rows.text: Positions a supportive device against the soles of the feet to hold the ankles in neutral alignment
rows.rationale: Foot drop is a plantar flexion contracture, the ankle setting with the toes pointed. This is the second action in the set aimed at contracture, because two different measures prevent the same complication.

questions.takeaway: Immobility damages seven systems through three mechanisms: stasis of fluids, pressure on tissue, and disuse of muscle, bone, and joint. Name the mechanism and the matching intervention follows.

questions.stem: Complete each sentence by selecting from the choices below.
questions.sentence:
A patient reports knee pain and instability after a twisting injury. The knee is swollen and the patient cannot fully straighten it.

The study that will show whether a bone is broken is [[1]].

The imaging is clear, but the pain and the instability continue. The study best able to show a torn ligament is [[2]].

A fracture is still suspected even though the imaging looked normal. The study that may reveal it is [[3]].

options.text: an x-ray
options.rationale: An x-ray passes radiation through tissue and shows dense structures clearly. It is the first study for a possible broken bone because it answers that question quickly.

options.text: a computed tomography scan
options.rationale: Computed tomography builds cross-sectional images and gives more detail of bone than a plain film. It earns its place with complex fractures, once a fracture is known or strongly suspected.

options.text: an ultrasound
options.rationale: Ultrasound uses sound waves and can assess tendons, muscles, fluid collections, and some joint abnormalities. Bone reflects the sound, so it is not the study for a suspected fracture.

options.text: magnetic resonance imaging
options.rationale: Magnetic resonance imaging shows soft tissue best. This is the right study for a different question in the same knee.

options.text: a computed tomography scan
options.rationale: Computed tomography is the detailed bone study. This is the near miss, because both this and the correct answer are cross-sectional and both sound like more information than an x-ray.

options.text: a bone scan
options.rationale: A bone scan detects areas of increased bone activity, such as occult fractures, infection, or tumors. A ligament tear does not light up a bone scan.

options.text: magnetic resonance imaging
options.rationale: Magnetic resonance imaging is best for soft tissue, including muscles, ligaments, tendons, cartilage, spinal structures, and bone marrow. Persistent instability with clear plain imaging points at ligament rather than bone.

options.text: a dual-energy x-ray absorptiometry scan
options.rationale: This scan measures bone mineral density and is used to assess osteoporosis. It answers a question about how strong bone is over time, not what tore today.

options.text: a bone scan
options.rationale: A bone scan detects areas of increased bone activity, and healing or injured bone is metabolically active. Occult means present but not visible on ordinary imaging, which is exactly the situation in this sentence.

options.text: a dual-energy x-ray absorptiometry scan
options.rationale: This scan measures bone mineral density. It reports how dense the bone is, which is a different question from whether this bone is cracked.

options.text: a computed tomography scan
options.rationale: Computed tomography provides more detailed bone images and is useful for complex fractures. This is the strongest distractor, because more detail sounds like the way to find something that is hiding.

options.text: an ultrasound
options.rationale: Ultrasound assesses tendons, muscles, fluid collections, and some joint abnormalities. No, sound does not penetrate bone well enough to answer that.

questions.takeaway: Match the study to the tissue and to the question. X-ray for a suspected break, computed tomography for detail on bone, magnetic resonance imaging for soft tissue, bone scan for a fracture nothing else has shown, and dual-energy absorptiometry for density.

questions.stem: A patient has 5 of 5 muscle strength in both legs but sways and grabs the bedrail when standing with eyes closed. Which system is most likely impaired?

options.text: Skeletal muscle strength
options.rationale: Already measured as full. Strength is not the failing component.

options.text: Joint range of motion
options.rationale: Limits how far a joint moves. It does not produce instability at rest in standing.

options.text: Bone density
options.rationale: Affects fracture risk, not postural control.

options.text: Proprioception and balance
options.rationale: Proprioception is awareness of body position without looking. Losing vision removes the backup, so the sway appears.

questions.takeaway: Strength and balance fail separately. A strong patient can still be unsafe to walk.

questions.stem: Which outcome does proper body alignment produce?

options.text: Reduced stress on joints and less fatigue
options.rationale: Alignment lets bone carry weight through bone. Poor alignment makes muscle hold the load, and muscle tires.

options.text: Increased muscle bulk
options.rationale: Bulk comes from loading the muscle, not from posture.

options.text: Faster wound healing
options.rationale: Unrelated to the mechanical effects of alignment.

options.text: Improved appetite
options.rationale: Not among the outcomes of alignment.

questions.takeaway: Alignment promotes efficient movement, minimizes joint stress, reduces fatigue, and improves balance.

questions.stem: During the Bedside Mobility Assessment Tool, a patient cannot sit at the side of the bed unassisted and is unable to reach across midline. Which level applies?

options.text: Level 2, maximum assist
options.rationale: Assigned when a patient sits successfully but cannot extend the leg and point the toes.

options.text: Level 1, total assist
options.rationale: Failing the sit and shake test means trunk strength and seated balance are inadequate. The assessment stops here.

options.text: Level 3, moderate assist
options.rationale: Assigned when a patient cannot lift the buttocks off the bed. This patient never reached that test.

options.text: Level 4, minimum assist
options.rationale: Requires advancing a step, which is three tests away.

questions.takeaway: You stop at the first test the patient cannot complete, and that failure names the level.

questions.stem: A patient is unconscious after a traumatic brain injury and cannot initiate any movement. Which exercise maintains joint flexibility?

options.text: Active range of motion
options.rationale: Requires the patient to move the joint. This patient cannot initiate movement.

options.text: Active-assistive range of motion
options.rationale: Requires the patient to start the movement so the nurse can complete it.

options.text: Passive range of motion
options.rationale: The nurse moves the joint entirely. It maintains flexibility and prevents contractures when the patient can contribute nothing.

options.text: Isometric exercise
options.rationale: Requires voluntary muscle contraction.

questions.takeaway: Passive is correct only when the patient cannot contribute. It maintains flexibility and builds no strength.

questions.stem: Which musculoskeletal changes are expected with aging? Select all that apply.

options.text: Muscle tissue atrophy
options.rationale: Muscle mass declines with age, contributing to weakness and slowed movement.

options.text: Decreased range of motion
options.rationale: Cartilage becomes less elastic and compressible, so joints move through a smaller arc.

options.text: Increased cartilage elasticity
options.rationale: The change runs the other way. Cartilage becomes less elastic.

options.text: Slowed movement
options.rationale: A named age-related change and part of why balance recovery takes longer.

options.text: Osteopenia or osteoporosis
options.rationale: Bone density falls, which is why height loss and fracture risk rise.

questions.takeaway: Expected aging changes are not the same as disease, and they still raise injury risk.

questions.stem: A nurse assesses a casted arm and cannot palpate the radial pulse. Which action does the nurse take next?

options.text: Document the finding and recheck in one hour
options.rationale: Delays confirmation of whether blood is reaching the hand.

options.text: Elevate the arm above the level of the heart
options.rationale: Raising a limb that may already be underperfused reduces arterial inflow further.

options.text: Apply warm compresses to improve circulation
options.rationale: Does not address a possible obstruction and delays the assessment.

options.text: Use a Doppler to check for flow, then compare with the other arm
options.rationale: A Doppler detects flow that cannot be felt. Comparing sides turns an uncertain finding into a clear one.

questions.takeaway: Absent or diminished pulses is a red flag. Confirm with Doppler and always compare sides.

questions.stem: A patient with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease wants to begin an exercise program. Which modification does the nurse anticipate?

options.text: Shorter sessions paced to the patient's tolerance with rest periods
options.rationale: Activity plans are modified rather than cancelled in chronic illness, and tolerance sets the pace.

options.text: Avoid all physical activity to conserve oxygen
options.rationale: Inactivity worsens deconditioning and breathlessness over time.

options.text: High-intensity intervals to build endurance quickly
options.rationale: Exceeds tolerance and risks severe dyspnea.

options.text: Exercise only while receiving nebulizer treatments
options.rationale: Not a standard modification and unnecessarily restricts when the patient can move.

questions.takeaway: Activity plans are modified in coronary artery disease, hypertension, COPD, diabetes, and immobility.

questions.stem: Which question best establishes a patient's mobility baseline on admission?

options.text: Are you afraid of falling here?
options.rationale: Assesses fear, which is worth knowing and is not a baseline of function.

options.text: Do you use any assistive devices at home?
options.rationale: Identifies what the patient normally relies on, which defines the starting point for the plan.

options.text: Would you like help getting up?
options.rationale: Offers assistance before any assessment has been done.

options.text: Has anyone in your family had a hip fracture?
options.rationale: Family history contributes nothing to this patient's current function.

questions.takeaway: Start every mobility assessment at baseline, then look for what is new.

questions.stem: A patient three days past abdominal surgery tolerates sitting upright at the edge of the mattress for several minutes and shakes hands firmly. With both feet flat on the floor and the knees below hip level, the patient cannot extend either leg or flex the ankles. The patient insists on standing. Which action does the nurse take?

options.text: Allow a standing attempt with one person assisting, since sitting balance is intact
options.rationale: Sitting balance was demonstrated and leg strength was not. Standing is the next test, and this patient did not clear the one before it.

options.text: Document moderate assist and attempt a stand with a gait belt
options.rationale: Moderate assist is assigned when a patient cannot lift the buttocks off the bed. The assessment stopped before that test, so this level was never demonstrated.

options.text: Document maximum assist and use a device or additional staff for any transfer
options.rationale: Failing the stretch and point test means lower-extremity strength is inadequate to progress toward standing. The patient's willingness does not change the finding, and the level determines the equipment used.

options.text: Repeat the sitting portion of the assessment before proceeding
options.rationale: Sitting was already passed. Repeating a cleared test delays the transfer without adding information.

questions.takeaway: The tool stops at the first failure, and that failure sets the equipment. A patient's readiness to try is not a level.

questions.stem: During a mobility assessment a patient stands, holds the position, marches in place, and advances each foot forward and back. While doing so the patient repeatedly lets go of the walker to gesture and states there is no need for it. Which nursing action follows?

options.text: Document the patient as independent and remove the walker from the room
options.rationale: Physical performance was adequate and safety awareness was not. Removing the device acts on half the assessment.

options.text: Assign a lower mobility level because the walker was released
options.rationale: The level is set by what the patient can physically do. Letting go of the device is a safety finding to address, not a downgrade of demonstrated strength.

options.text: Restrict the patient to bed until a physical therapy evaluation is completed
options.rationale: Restriction produces the weakness the assessment exists to prevent, and the patient has just demonstrated the ability to step.

options.text: Ambulate with standby assistance and address the safety awareness before independence
options.rationale: Advancing a step meets the criterion for the highest level, and that level is assessed together with balance, stability, gait, and safety awareness. Strength is demonstrated and judgment is not, so supervision continues.

questions.takeaway: The walk test scores balance, stability, gait, and safety awareness. A strong patient with poor judgment is not independent.

questions.stem: A nurse tests upper extremity strength. The right arm lifts off the bed and holds against moderate downward pressure before giving way. The left arm lifts off the bed but drops as soon as any pressure is applied. How does the nurse document this?

options.text: Right 4 of 5, left 3 of 5
options.rationale: Movement against some resistance is grade 4, and movement against gravity alone with no resistance tolerated is grade 3. Both cleared gravity, which puts both above grade 2.

options.text: Right 5 of 5, left 4 of 5
options.rationale: Full strength holds against firm resistance without giving way, and the right arm gave way under moderate pressure.

options.text: Right 4 of 5, left 2 of 5
options.rationale: Grade 2 is movement only when gravity is removed. The left arm lifted off the bed, so it cleared gravity.

options.text: Right 3 of 5, left 2 of 5
options.rationale: Understates both. Tolerating moderate resistance is above grade 3, and lifting against gravity is above grade 2.

questions.takeaway: Grade 3 is the gravity hinge. Below it the limb only moves in a supported plane, above it you are adding resistance.

questions.stem: Six hours after a below-knee cast was applied for a fibular fracture, a patient has pain rated 9 of 10 that increased after the last analgesic dose. The toes are swollen and cool, capillary refill is 5 seconds, and the patient reports the foot feels numb. The opposite foot is warm with refill under 2 seconds. Which action does the nurse take first?

options.text: Elevate the extremity above heart level to reduce the swelling
options.rationale: Elevation reduces swelling in a limb with intact perfusion. Raising a limb that is already underperfused lowers arterial inflow further.

options.text: Notify the provider immediately and keep the limb at heart level
options.rationale: Pain disproportionate to the injury and unrelieved by analgesia, with delayed refill, coolness, and new numbness on one side, is compromised perfusion. Keeping the limb level preserves arterial inflow while help is summoned.

options.text: Administer the next dose of analgesia and reassess in 30 minutes
options.rationale: Analgesia has already failed, which is data rather than a reason to repeat it. Thirty minutes is time the limb does not have.

options.text: Apply ice over the cast and document the neurovascular findings
options.rationale: Cold causes vasoconstriction in a limb with failing circulation, and documenting is not an intervention.

questions.takeaway: Pain out of proportion and unrelieved by opioids in a casted limb is a circulation problem until proven otherwise. Always compare sides.

questions.stem: A patient in the clinic has lost 5 cm of height over eight years, fractured a wrist catching a fall from standing, and reports mid-back pain that began without injury. Which diagnostic study does the nurse anticipate?

options.text: Magnetic resonance imaging of the thoracic spine
options.rationale: Best for soft tissue such as ligaments, cartilage, cord, and marrow. It will not answer whether bone density is low.

options.text: Computed tomography of the wrist
options.rationale: Gives detailed bone images for mapping a complex fracture. The fracture is already known and is not the underlying question.

options.text: Dual-energy x-ray absorptiometry
options.rationale: Height loss, a fracture from a low-energy fall, and atraumatic back pain together point to reduced bone density. This scan measures bone mineral density and is the study used to assess osteoporosis.

options.text: A bone scan
options.rationale: Detects increased bone activity such as an occult fracture, infection, or tumor. It does not measure how dense the bone is.

questions.takeaway: Read the findings as a group. Height loss plus a fragility fracture plus atraumatic pain is a density question, not an imaging-the-injury question.

questions.stem: A patient with several weeks of progressive proximal muscle weakness has a creatine kinase of 4200 units/L, an elevated aldolase, and an elevated aspartate aminotransferase. The alkaline phosphatase and bilirubin are normal. What do these results support?

options.text: Hepatic injury
options.rationale: Aspartate aminotransferase is found in both liver and muscle, which is why the stem includes the other liver studies. Normal alkaline phosphatase and bilirubin make a liver source unlikely.

options.text: Reduced bone mineral density
options.rationale: Measured by a density scan. These are muscle enzymes and say nothing about bone.

options.text: An inflammatory joint process
options.rationale: Assessed by imaging and joint fluid analysis. Weakness described as proximal and enzymes from muscle point away from the joints.

options.text: Muscle tissue damage
options.rationale: These enzymes are released from injured muscle cells. Normal alkaline phosphatase and bilirubin argue against a liver source for the elevated aminotransferase, which leaves muscle.

questions.takeaway: Creatine kinase, aldolase, lactate dehydrogenase, and aspartate aminotransferase rise with muscle damage. The other liver values are what separate muscle from liver.

questions.stem: A patient of 62 with a family history of osteoporosis asks how to protect bone and muscle over the coming years. Which recommendations does the nurse include? Select all that apply.

options.text: Weight-bearing activity such as walking on most days
options.rationale: Loading bone is what keeps mineral in it, and loading muscle is what maintains strength. Both are named among the measures that promote musculoskeletal health.

options.text: Adequate calcium and vitamin D intake
options.rationale: Appropriate intake is listed among the measures that maintain bone over time.

options.text: Stopping tobacco use
options.rationale: Avoiding tobacco is named directly among the measures that promote musculoskeletal health.

options.text: Limiting alcohol intake
options.rationale: Excessive alcohol is to be limited, and it also contributes to falls and to poor nutrition.

options.text: Switching from walking to swimming to spare the joints
options.rationale: Swimming is good conditioning and removes the weight bearing that maintains bone density. It supplements rather than replaces.

options.text: Adding a daily calcium supplement regardless of dietary intake
options.rationale: The recommendation is appropriate intake, which accounts for what the diet already supplies rather than adding a supplement automatically.

questions.takeaway: Activity, weight bearing, nutrition, calcium and vitamin D, no tobacco, limited alcohol. Non-weight-bearing exercise does not protect bone.

questions.stem: Two patients are assessed on the same morning. Patient one has 5 of 5 strength in all extremities and full range of motion but cannot rise from a chair without using both armrests and stops twice crossing the room. Patient two has 4 of 5 strength and mildly reduced shoulder range but dresses, transfers, and walks the hallway without stopping. Which statement about their functional ability is accurate?

options.text: Patient two has the higher functional ability, because functional ability is measured by tasks accomplished
options.rationale: Functional ability is what the patient can do: turn, sit unsupported, stand, transfer, walk, and perform activities of daily living. Strength and range are components, and neither predicts performance on its own.

options.text: Patient one has the higher functional ability, because strength and range of motion are normal
options.rationale: Those are two measurements taken at rest. This patient cannot rise unaided or cross a room without stopping, which is what function measures.

options.text: The two patients have equivalent functional ability
options.rationale: One completes daily tasks without stopping and the other cannot. The difference is exactly what a functional assessment captures.

options.text: Functional ability cannot be compared without a formal strength grade for both
options.rationale: Both strength grades are given, and function is assessed by observing tasks rather than by grading muscles.

questions.takeaway: Strength is a number at rest. Function is what the patient accomplishes, and the two come apart in real patients.
